body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Adherence to daily spontaneous awakening trials under a nurse-driven protocol: a two-year observational study in three intensive care units","authors":"Brandvold-Mensah K, Iwasaki-Oyelaran T, Carvalho-Dunn R","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Critical Care Nursing Practice","doi":"10.5555/jccnp.2020.0187","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 5,940 eligible ventilated patient-days in three intensive care units using a nurse-driven sedation interruption protocol. An awakening trial was performed on 44 percent of eligible days. The most common documented reasons for not performing it were overnight agitation (31 percent of missed days) and planned procedures (18 percent), and 22 percent of missed days had no documented reason. Units that kept a paper checklist at the bedside performed trials on 58 percent of eligible days against 37 percent in the unit without one. Adherence did not change over the two years."},{"title":"Pairing awakening and breathing trials: coordination between nurses and respiratory therapists","authors":"Okafor-Lindqvist A, Ruiz-Hallberg M","year":2018,"venue":"Ventilation Practice Review","doi":"10.5555/rcci.2018.0049","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In one medical intensive care unit, awakening trials by nurses and breathing trials by respiratory therapists were scheduled separately and rarely paired. The unit agreed a shared 08:00 time for both trials and a bedside card that the nurse handed to the therapist when the awakening trial passed. Over nine months the proportion of eligible patient-days with a paired trial rose from 22 percent to 49 percent, and median ventilator days fell from 6.1 to 5.2. The comparison was before and after, and the unit's case mix changed during the period."},{"title":"Value stream mapping of the morning sedation interruption process in an intensive care unit","authors":"Grieve-Achebe S, Varadi-Lund H","year":2022,"venue":"Lean Health Operations","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Nurses, respiratory therapists and physicians mapped the morning sedation interruption process in a 20-bed intensive care unit. The map showed 11 steps and four waits, the longest being physician approval before a nurse could stop sedation (median 47 minutes), which often ran into rounds. The team removed the approval step for patients who passed the safety screen and moved the screen to 06:30. Over 16 weeks, completed interruptions on eligible days rose from 35 percent to 63 percent. The evaluation was an uncontrolled before-after comparison without follow-up beyond 16 weeks."},{"title":"Why nurses do not interrupt sedation: a qualitative study of decision making at the bedside","authors":"Lemaire-Osei N, Harcourt-Tanaka J","year":2019,"venue":"Bedside Critical Care Nursing Studies","doi":"10.5555/nccr.2019.0133","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We spoke with 21 critical care nurses in two units about mornings when they did not interrupt sedation for an eligible patient. Nurses described fear of self-extubation and of an agitated patient harming themselves, reluctance when family members were present, pressure to have patients ready for rounds, and uncertainty about whether they could stop sedation without a physician's agreement. Several said the protocol's safety screen was clear but that the decision to act on it felt like a personal risk. Nurses with more than five years of experience interrupted sedation more readily."},{"title":"Safety of nurse-driven sedation interruption: self-extubation and agitation events across 4,200 interruptions","authors":"Petrov-Nwosu D, Castellanos-Whitby E, Sato-Mbeki L","year":2016,"venue":"Critical Care Safety Review","doi":"10.5555/ccsr.2016.0071","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We recorded adverse events during 4,200 nurse-driven sedation interruptions in four intensive care units over three years. Self-extubation occurred in 0.6 percent of interruptions and was not more frequent than on days without interruption in the same patients. Agitation requiring a bolus dose occurred in 9 percent of interruptions and usually settled within 30 minutes. No self-extubation led to reintubation after more than one hour. Events were recorded by the bedside nurse, and events on days without interruption may have been under-reported."},{"title":"Sedation interruption protocols, adherence and ventilator days: a systematic review","authors":"Rahman-Ellis T, Lindgren-Obi F, Moreau-Kamara S","year":2021,"venue":"Critical Care Evidence Syntheses","doi":"10.5555/cces.2021.0215","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We included 17 trials and 12 observational studies of daily sedation interruption or nurse-driven sedation protocols. In trials, daily interruption was associated with fewer ventilator days (mean difference -1.2 days), but adherence in trials was about 80 percent of eligible days, while routine practice studies reported adherence between 30 and 55 percent. Implementation strategies were described in only nine studies and were too varied to compare. The authors conclude that the gap between trial and routine adherence limits the benefit patients receive in practice."},{"title":"Electronic reminders for daily sedation interruption: an interrupted time series","authors":"Ferreira-Holt J, Nakashima-Oduya R","year":2024,"venue":"Journal of Critical Care Nursing Practice","doi":"10.5555/jccnp.2024.0058","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"An intensive care unit added an electronic reminder that prompted the bedside nurse at 06:00 to complete the sedation safety screen. In an interrupted time series over 18 months, documented screening rose from 62 percent to 88 percent of eligible days, but completed interruptions changed little, from 36 percent to 39 percent. Chart review showed that nurses documented the screen and then deferred the interruption until after rounds. The authors conclude that reminders improved documentation rather than practice and that the barriers lay later in the morning process."}]}
